question: Tell me about a time you supported moving a high performer to another team, even though you needed them. What drove that decision?

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you supported moving a high performer to another team, even though you needed them. What drove that decision?

On my team last year we had a strong engineer who was doing well on our project but wanted to switch to mobile development. I helped connect them with the mobile team lead and supported the transfer even though we were in the middle of a release.
What made you decide to support it instead of trying to keep them?

They had already shown they could deliver on backend, and I figured the mobile experience would make them stronger overall. I talked to my manager and we agreed the short-term gap was worth it for their growth.
How did you handle the workload after they left?
We shifted some tickets and I took on a couple extra ones myself for two sprints until we hired a replacement.

junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Hire and Develop the Best for a junior. The candidate described actively supporting a transfer mid-release because they believed the move would strengthen the person's skills long-term. They explicitly weighed the short-term pain against the individual's development and coordinated with their manager before acting. Workload was absorbed personally for two sprints rather than blocking the move. This shows early ownership of developing others even at individual-contributor scope. The main gap is that impact stayed local with no evidence of influencing peers or processes around talent movement.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you supported moving a high performer to another team, even though you needed them. What drove that decision?
Last year my best backend engineer wanted to move into platform work. I sponsored the transfer even though we were two people short on a critical service.
How did you make the case internally?
I met with the platform director and my own manager, laid out the skills gap it would create, and proposed a six-week knowledge transfer plan plus backfill request.
What was the outcome for the person and the team?
They shipped two platform projects in the first quarter and later helped us with a cross-team incident. We hired their replacement in eight weeks.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you supported moving a high performer to another team, even though you needed them. What drove that decision?
Two years ago our top engineering manager wanted to run a new product area. I supported the move even though it left a gap in our core org during a reorg.
What trade-offs did you consider at the org level?
I modeled the retention risk if we blocked strong leaders from growth opportunities and the downstream impact on hiring if we became known as a place that holds people back.
How did you handle the leadership gap?
I accelerated two internal promotions and created a dotted-line support structure for six months while the new area launched.

exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Hire and Develop the Best for an exec. The candidate supported the move of a top engineering manager during a reorg after modeling retention risk and external hiring brand damage. They responded by accelerating two promotions and establishing temporary dotted-line structures rather than blocking the opportunity. This reflects strategic judgment on long-term org health over short-term leadership coverage. The decision was framed around scalable talent practices, not individual heroics. The main gap is that the story centers on one high-profile case without evidence of embedding this approach into recurring org processes or metrics.
